newsletter_intro:
Gamay is such a good reminder that wine does not have to be serious to be interesting. This grape is light on its feet, full of personality, and way more versatile than people give it credit for.

If you’ve only heard of Beaujolais Nouveau, this one is worth a proper look.

If you’ve only ever thought of Beaujolais as the November release, there is a lot more here. Which Gamay style are you most curious about?

instagram_reel.hook: Gamay is the grape that refuses to be serious — and honestly, that’s why people love it.
instagram_reel.script:
Let’s talk about Gamay, because this grape deserves more love.

You might hear Gamay called Gamay Noir, or even just Beaujolais, but it’s the same grape. It usually makes wines that are lighter in body, bright in acidity, and full of red berry fruit.

Beaujolais is where Gamay really became famous, and it gives you a whole range — from easy, fresh bottles to more serious crus that can age and build real structure.

And yes, Beaujolais Nouveau is fun. But it is the party version. If you want to see what Gamay can really do, look at the crus.

Also, this grape works beautifully with a slight chill. That alone makes it very easy to love.

tiktok.hook: Gamay is the red wine for people who don’t want red wine to be a whole personality.
tiktok.script:
Okay, Gamay needs a little more hype.

This is the grape behind Beaujolais, and you may also hear it called Gamay Noir. Same grape, different name.

What does it taste like? Usually lighter-bodied, bright in acidity, and very red-fruit forward — think cherry, strawberry, that kind of energy.

And here’s the fun part: Beaujolais Nouveau is not the whole story. It’s the festive, drink-it-now version. The crus are where Gamay gets deeper, more structured, and honestly more interesting.

If you want a red that can handle a slight chill, Gamay is a great one to know.
tiktok.caption: Gamay is way more than just Beaujolais Nouveau. If you like bright, juicy reds, this one should be on your radar.

linkedin.post:
Gamay is one of the clearest examples of why wine education should feel inviting, not intimidating.

It’s a grape that is often introduced through Beaujolais Nouveau, which can make people think they already know the story. But Gamay has much more to offer than a once-a-year release.

From the approachable everyday bottles of Beaujolais and Beaujolais Villages to the more structured, age-worthy crus, Gamay shows real range. It is also a grape that travels well, with interesting expressions in the Loire, Switzerland, and here in Ontario.

For trade, that versatility matters. It gives us an easy entry point for guests who want something fresh, lighter, and food-friendly, while also opening the door to more serious conversation about terroir, village identity, and cellar potential.

And from a service perspective, Gamay is a gift. It is approachable, flexible, and works beautifully with a slight chill — which makes it especially useful when the weather warms up and guests want a red that feels easy without being simple.
